summary: Describes how to carry structured NxDS0 TDM signals, as used in telephone networks, over packet networks as pseudowires. It is the structure-aware companion to RFC 4553. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Old phone lines carry voice in fixed time slots. This shows how to put those slots into internet-style packets while keeping them organized.

questions: how do you send tdm circuits over packet networks
what is the difference between structured and unstructured tdm emulation
how does cesopsn preserve timing and alarms
subtitle: Carrying structured phone network signals over packet networks while preserving the time slot structure.

tldr.problem: Legacy phone networks use Time Division Multiplexed (TDM) circuits with fixed time slot structures. Moving to packet networks requires preserving this structure for compatibility and to enable DS0-level grooming.
tldr.mechanism: CESoPSN (Circuit Emulation Service over Packet Switched Network) encapsulates structured NxDS0 TDM signals into packets using the PWE3 pseudowire architecture. It preserves the time slot structure, includes optional RTP timing headers, and handles signaling separately.
tldr.outcome: This informational specification allows phone networks to continue using TDM equipment while transitioning to packet-based backhaul, with better bandwidth efficiency than structure-agnostic encapsulation.

today: RFC 5086 is an Informational document that continues to be used by service providers emulating TDM circuits over modern packet networks. It has not been obsoleted and complements RFC 4553, which handles structure-agnostic TDM emulation.

sections.title: Emulating Structured TDM
sections.content:
Legacy telephone networks use Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) where multiple conversations share one circuit by taking turns in fixed time slots. When moving these circuits to packet networks, the question is how to preserve that structure.

RFC 4553 handled this in a structure-agnostic way: converting the entire TDM bit stream to packets without preserving slot boundaries. RFC 5086 takes a different approach: structure-aware emulation that preserves the time slot structure. This enables switching systems to see and manipulate individual time slots (DS0 channels), and improves efficiency through DS0-level grooming and cross-connect applications.

CESoPSN (Circuit Emulation Service over Packet Switched Network) is part of the Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3) architecture, which treats packet network segments as transparent point-to-point connections.
sections.plainLanguage: A telephone circuit has 24 or 30 time slots. One way to send it over the internet is to treat it as a stream of bits. Another way is to send the time slots as numbered packets. This memo explains the numbered way.

sections.title: Packet Structure and Encapsulation
sections.content:
A CESoPSN packet consists of a control word (4 bytes), an optional RTP header (12 bytes), and a payload containing TDM data. The packet structure varies depending on whether it runs over MPLS, UDP/IP, or L2TPv3.

For UDP/IP networks, the RTP header comes immediately after the UDP header (for header compression compatibility). For MPLS networks, the control word follows the MPLS label stack immediately. For L2TPv3, the control word follows the L2TPv3 header.

The CESoPSN Control Word carries status flags and a sequence number. The L bit marks abnormal attachment circuit conditions; the M field (2 bits) distinguishes signaling packets and carries remote alarm information; the R bit indicates packet loss state at the receive side. The length field carries the packet size if under 64 bytes; otherwise it is zero.

The RTP header, when used, carries a timestamp derived from the recovered clock of the incoming TDM circuit (absolute mode) or from a common timing source (differential mode). The timestamp clock must be an integer multiple of 8 kHz; all implementations support 8 kHz.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet has a 4-byte header with status flags and a number. If you want to send timing information, you add a 12-byte RTP header. Then you put the actual time slot data in the payload.

sections.title: Payload Structure and Services
sections.content:
CESoPSN preserves TDM's basic structure: groups of time slots that repeat at 8000 frames per second. Each CESoPSN packet carries the same number of octets (bytes) in both directions, ensuring constant packetization latency. The payload is filled with TDM data in the same order as on the original circuit, starting from the most significant bit.

Basic NxDS0 services carry N time slots from the same frame (or multiple frames from the same originating trunk). The payload is aligned with packet boundaries: structures start at the beginning of the payload, and the total TDM data per packet is an integer multiple of the basic structure size.

Services with signaling (like Channel-Associated Signaling, CAS) can be carried in the same packets as TDM data or in separate signaling packets. The common data path and packet format remain unchanged for TDM data regardless of signaling presence.

Invalid TDM data (when loss of signal, out-of-frame, or alarm conditions exist) can be omitted to save bandwidth, with the L bit set in the control word to signal this condition.
sections.plainLanguage: You always send the same number of time slot bytes in each packet. The bytes go in the same order as on the phone circuit. If you need to send signaling information (like dial tones), you send it in separate packets or mixed with the data, but the regular data packets stay the same.

sections.title: Operation and Defect Handling
sections.content:
The Interworking Function (IWF) at each endpoint segments TDM data into packets (PSN-bound direction) and reconstitutes TDM from packets (CE-bound direction). It monitors for defects and packet loss.

CESoPSN implements detection of lost packets through sequence numbering. When consecutive packets are lost (configurable threshold), the IWF sets the R bit to signal packet loss state to the remote side. When packets resume, the R bit is cleared.

The control word flags (L and M bits) carry TDM alarm signals across the network: Loss of Signal (LOS), Out of Frame (OOF), Alarm Indication Signal (AIS), and Remote Alarm Indication (RAI). These allow the far-end equipment to see the same defects as the near-end network interface.

End-to-end delay should be constant between a pair of Customer Edge (CE) devices regardless of the emulated service bit rate. Packetization latency ranges from 1 to 5 milliseconds, configurable in 125-microsecond increments.
sections.plainLanguage: At each end, a device takes phone data in and puts it in packets (or takes packets and puts phone data out). It watches for lost packets and counts them with a sequence number. It also sends alarm signals from the phone network into the packets so the far end knows if something is wrong.

sections.title: QoS and Constraints
sections.content:
CESoPSN packets must fit within the path MTU between endpoints. IPv4 implementations must set the Don't Fragment flag. The total packet size is the CESoPSN header (including optional RTP header) plus the TDM payload.

To maintain constant delay and support circuit emulation, the PSN must provide appropriate Quality of Service. Congestion control mechanisms vary by network type: MPLS networks can use traffic engineering, UDP/IP networks can use lower priorities or traffic shaping.

The sequence number provides lost-packet detection but not recovery; lost packets cannot be retransmitted in real-time TDM circuits. The design assumes the underlying PSN handles congestion and loss appropriately for voice or data circuits.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet has to be small enough to fit on the network. The network needs to carry the packets without too much delay or loss, since you can't ask a phone conversation to wait for a late packet.
